q1: SELECT DISTINCT AUTHOR_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS WHERE AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT(V1.AUTHOR_ID) AS ID FROM VIEWS V1, VIEWS V2 WHERE V1.AUTHOR_ID = V2.VIEWER_ID AND V1.VIEWER_ID = V2.VIEWER_ID ORDER BY ID
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT AUTHOR_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS WHERE AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID ORDER BY ID
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT(V1.AUTHOR_ID) AS ID FROM VIEWS V1, VIEWS V2 WHERE V1.AUTHOR_ID = V2.VIEWER_ID AND V1.VIEWER_ID = V2.VIEWER_ID ORDER BY ID
counterexample:
INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (1, 1, 1, '2023-01-01');
INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (2, 2, 3, '2023-01-02');
explanation: Q1 finds distinct AUTHOR_IDs where AUTHOR_ID equals VIEWER_ID. Q2 finds distinct AUTHOR_IDs from V1 where V1.AUTHOR_ID equals V2.VIEWER_ID and V1.VIEWER_ID equals V2.VIEWER_ID, which effectively finds AUTHOR_IDs that match VIEWER_IDs in another row (not necessarily the same row). These two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: A test database with one row where AUTHOR_ID = VIEWER_ID and another row where AUTHOR_ID != VIEWER_ID will show Q1 returning one row and Q2 returning zero rows.
